results.summary: This design is a synthesized time-to-digital converter (TDC) that measures the time interval between two input signals using two Vernier delay rings with slightly different delays. It captures the time difference on the rising edge of the stop signal and outputs the result in 8-bit chunks, selectable via input pins. The design is intended for high-resolution time measurement, with an analog-simulated resolution of about 6 ps. It requires external signal generators with nanosecond resolution to provide the start and stop signals, and it is notable for being implemented entirely with standard cells.

This project implements an on-chip temperature sensor synthesized from standard cells. It measures the chip temperature and outputs the result, with a debug mode that allows direct control of the sensor's DAC and enable signals. The design is intended to be used by simply powering it on and observing the digital outputs, though a logic analyzer is recommended for inspection. The documentation is minimal, stating that a better explanation will be provided in the future, but the pin descriptions and debug instructions provide enough detail to understand its operation.

This is a tiny time-to-digital converter (TDC) constructed entirely from standard cells, using a Skywater130 FA-2 delay element. It measures the time between launch and capture clocks and outputs a 7-bit hardware value along with a valid signal. The design includes power-gating control signals and is intended to be tested using VCS simulation with gate-level netlists. External hardware is not required beyond connecting the pins, and the design is notable for its all-standard-cell implementation and inclusion of power-gating features.

This is a 4-bit flash analog-to-digital converter (ADC) that uses a resistor ladder to generate 15 reference voltages and comparators to produce a unary output, which is then encoded into binary using a digital encoder with error correction. It includes debug modes to independently test the ADC and the encoder, and provides additional outputs for monitoring unary bits and XOR/mux functions. The design requires an analog input voltage between 0 and 1.8 V, and can be tested with a simple potentiometer or a microcontroller-generated PWM signal with an RC filter. Silicon tests have confirmed its functionality, with testers observing correct operation using sine waves and manual sweeping.

This design implements an anomaly detection system using an isolation tree algorithm, intended for integration into SoCs with AI accelerators. It consists of an input buffer that collects sensor data bit-by-bit, and a state machine that processes the data to detect anomalies based on a predefined byte pattern. The design is currently simplistic, checking against a set pattern, but is intended to be expanded to more complex algorithms. It requires a binary output sensor as external hardware and is designed for real-time anomaly detection in embedded applications.

This project is a keypad controller that scans a 4x4 keypad by driving columns and reading rows to detect key presses. The detected key is decoded and displayed on a single 7-segment display. The design operates at a low clock frequency of 1000 Hz and requires an external keypad PMOD connected to the bidirectional pins. It is a simple interface project intended for experimenting with keypad input and display output.

This design implements a memory game similar to Simon, where the device plays a sequence of button-lamp colors and the player must repeat the sequence by pressing corresponding buttons. The game keeps a high score until power is lost or reset, and ends when the player makes a mistake, waits too long, or reaches 32 moves. It requires four buttons and four lamps connected to the specified pins, plus a start button. The design is notable for its simple implementation of a classic game with high-score tracking and visual feedback.

This is a tiny 8-bit CPU with an SPI Flash and PSRAM controller, designed to execute programs stored in external SPI Flash and use PSRAM for data memory. It includes GPIO pins for general-purpose I/O and a dedicated SPI transmitter. The CPU loads instructions from address 0x0000 on the SPI Flash after reset, and a macro assembler is available for programming. External hardware includes SPI Flash and optionally SPI PSRAM, and the design is notable for its compact integration of a CPU with external memory controllers.
